6 We join AAF and other departments in advancing a more diverse, inclusive, and anti-racist university that will better serve our community of students, faculty, administrators, and staff. 2.

GWS becoming a department does not impact other departments and programs.
As discussed above, GWS has operated as a department for many years without impacting other academic units.
Rather, GWS has collaborated closely with other academic units to uphold its interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary discipline.
With department designation, GWS will fortify and broaden collaboration across the disciplines.
D.
INTERINSTITUTIONAL CONSIDERATIONS: The organizational change should be consistent with all policies of the Council on Postsecondary Education pertaining to the coordination and collaboration between public institutions of higher education. 1.

Estimate the projected impact of the organizational change on the other public higher education institutions in Rhode Island (e.g., loss of students or revenues), provide a specific rationale of the assumptions make in the projections, and indicate the manner in which the other public institutions were consulted in developing the projections.
Have you communicated with other institutions about the organizational change and have any concerns been raised related to role, scope, and mission or duplication?
URI will lead the way in RI by creating a Department of Gender and Women's Studies.
Regionally, there are several departments that include UMass-Dartmouth, Connecticut College, Wellesley College, and Simmons College.
None of our similar peer institutions has departments in Women's Studies (JMU, UNH, UVM, etc.).
Of our "aspire to be like" peer institutions, the University of Delaware and University of Virginia have departments in Women's Studies, UCONN does not.
This moment offers an ideal opportunity for URI to take a leadership position by designating GWS as a department and rise to the level of two out of three "aspiring to be like" institutions.

There will be no impacts to other RI institutions in terms of loss of students or revenue.
Nearly 99% of our majors come from within URI and select GWS as a second major in their sophomore year or as a first semester junior.
All major RI public and private institutions offer Women's Studies or similar programs like Gender and Sexuality Studies.
These institutions have successfully recruited students for their programs over the years.
There is no reason to believe that a change in GWS designation as a department will change that pattern. 2.

GWS does not require new facilities and capital equipment for this change.

GWS has been housed in Roosevelt Hall since its establishment as a program in 1978.
GWS will remain at its current location on the third floor of Roosevelt Hall and occupy the same offices of 317, 315, 313, 311, 316 and 314.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #2026-2027-01 October 15, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting - FOR ACTION (Introduced at the September 17, 2026 Faculty Senate Meeting) Creates standard process for committee formation Approved by FSEC 08/31/26 and 10/7/26 (as amended) Reviewed by CBUM 09/28/26 and 10/8/26 (as amended) Legislation effective date: Spring semester 2027 Rationale: The limited number of faculty senators, in combination with University-Manual-mandated committee staffing requirements, can make it difficult to staff an expanding number of standing committees.
This makes it important to ensure that additional standing committees and subcommittees, whose charges and memberships are proscribed in the University Manual, are created only in response to a significant and sustained need.
In contrast, special committees can be created by the Faculty Senate to address pressing issues.
While there is no limit to the length of time a special committee can exist, the faculty senate must vote to reauthorize each special committee each year.

This legislation mandates that a newly formed committee must exist as a special committee for at least three (3) years before legislation reconstituting it as a standing committee or subcommittee can be considered by the Faculty Senate.
Such legislation must be accompanied by language specifying the charge and membership of the standing committee for inclusion in the University Manual.
This change provides time for the Faculty Senate to 1) consider whether a new standing committee or subcommittee is truly warranted; and 2) craft an appropriate and achievable charge for the body.
This legislation does not mandate that a special committee must be reconstituted as a standing committee after three years.
It is also not retroactive, i.e., all existing standing committees and subcommittees remain unchanged.
This original version of this legislation was introduced for discussion at the 9/17/26 Faculty Senate meeting.
The final version has been revised as follows in response to faculty/staff comments. 1.
Remove language mentioning joint committees .
Joint committees are, by definition, created in concert with the administration (staffing, wording, charge, power balance).

While the faculty and administration may choose to designate a joint committee as a special joint committee subject to the rules and procedures detailed below, the power to do so does not rest exclusively with the faculty senate. 2.
Identify the assessment process and who conducts it.
Added language to §4.12.1 specifying that the Special Committee’s self-assessment shall be reviewed by FSEC.
FSEC which shall use it as the basis for a recommendation to the Faculty Senate to vote on whether the 1

Committee should dissolve, continue as a Special Committee, or be reconstituted as a permanent Standing Committee or Subcommittee. 3.
What happens if no reauthorization vote is taken before the end of the AY?
Added language to §4.11.1 specifying that all Special Committees are annually authorized by vote of the Faculty Senate.
A Special Committee that has not received an affirmative reauthorization vote (assuming that no duly authorized extension has been granted) within one year of authorization shall be dissolved. 4.
After the third-year review, can a reauthorized Special Committee apply to change its status?
Added language to §4.12.1 specifying that a Special Committee must wait at least two years after its third-year review (i.e., be in its fifth consecutive year of operation) before requesting that the Faculty Senate reconsider reconstituting it as a Standing Committee or Subcommittee.

What is the Capital Improvement Plan? • 5 Year plan that shows projects that have a total project cost of greater than $1 Million • It is a rolling plan that is submitted annually as a request to the state, typically on July 1st. Who Approves the Capital Improvement Plan? There are 5 levels of approval. They are: 1. University of Rhode Island ‐ Facilities Committee (April & May) 2. University of Rhode Island ‐ Senior Leadership (May & June) 3. University of Rhode Island ‐ Board of Trustees (June) 4. Executive Branch 1. Analysis performed and Recommendations made by the Office of Management and Budget (July‐December) 2. Final Approval by Governor’s Office (Third week of January) 5. Legislative Branch 1. Analysis performed and Recommendations made by both the House and Senate Fiscal Offices (January – June) 2. Final Plan approved as part of the RI Budget Appropriations Bill (June) How is a project added to the Capital Improvement Plan? • In order to receive consideration, all projects must be submitted on the Capital Improvement Request form by a member of the Senior Leadership to the URI Office of Planning & Real Estate Development • Most projects will have an advanced planning study performed prior to inclusion in the Capital Improvement plan to determine program, siting, massing, and, total expected project cost
What does the Capital Improvement Plan cover? The University of Rhode Island’s Board of Trustees is responsible for about 25% of the State’s total real estate portfolio.
